questions.question: Why is `container-type: inline-size` usually preferred over `container-type: size`?
options: `size` is not supported in any browser
`size` contains both axes, so the element needs an explicit height or it collapses, while `inline-size` lets height still grow with content
`inline-size` also enables media queries inside the element
`inline-size` makes the element query its own width
questions.explanation: Size containment on both axes means the element's height no longer comes from its children. inline-size only contains the width, which is what most component queries need.

questions.question: A `.card` has `container-type: inline-size` and an `@container (min-width: 30rem) { .card { ... } }` rule. Why might the rule never apply to `.card` itself?
options: Container queries only work with px units
The container must also have a container-name
An element cannot query itself; @container matches the nearest ancestor container, so the container should be a wrapper
@container rules must be placed inside a @layer
questions.explanation: Container queries style descendants of the container. To restyle the card, put container-type on its parent wrapper.

questions.question: Which selector styles a list as two columns only once it has five or more items, without JavaScript?
questions.explanation: If a fifth li child exists, the :has() argument matches, so the parent .list is selected. This is a quantity query built on :has().

questions.question: With `@layer base, components, utilities;` declared, which normal (non-important) declaration wins?
options: The one with the highest specificity, whatever layer it is in
A rule in the base layer, because it was declared first
A rule in components, because it is in the middle
An unlayered rule, which beats all layered rules regardless of specificity
questions.explanation: Among layers, later ones win over earlier ones before specificity is considered, and unlayered styles beat all layers for normal declarations. The order flips for !important.
